title: Renaissance
full_review:
Graphic novels are increasingly providing intriguing fodder for the movies -- "Sin City" and "V for Vendetta" being recent examples.

The futuristic "Renaissance" (Miramax) has an original screenplay (by Matthieu Delaporte and Alexandre de la Patelliere), but is essentially a stylish comic book come to life, rendered with "motion capture" animation technique.

Set in the Paris of 2054, the interesting tale revolves around young scientist Ilona (Romola Garai), the former protege of a renowned geneticist, Jonas Muller (Ian Holm), who works for the Avalon Corp., a sinister megacompany promising eternal youth and beauty.

When she is kidnapped, after visiting her older sister, Bislane (Catherine McCormack), in a nightclub, police detective Barthelemy Karas (authoritatively voiced by Daniel Craig) is assigned to rescue her.

He enlists Bislane's help, falling in love with her along the way, while fending off the malevolent forces of the company's vice president, Paul Dellenbach (Jonathan Pryce), with his own motives for finding her first.

Director Christian Volckman's debut feature film has a sometimes overly complex (and slightly tedious) plot that, in its essentials, we've seen before, but the striking black-and-white design (with just a bit of color in a couple of scenes), and committed acting by the mostly British voice talent holds your interest. The overall emotional impact is, nonetheless, on the cool side, perhaps limiting its popular appeal.

Several of the animators' concepts for this labyrinthine Paris -- a second-tier walkway outside Notre Dame Cathedral and Avalon billboards placed strategically around the city, for example -- are intriguing, and the familiar landmarks such as the Eiffel Tower are well drawn, too.

There are some interesting ethical conundrums along the way, though to talk about them would involve plot spoilers. But the script's position seems morally on target.

The violence and sexual elements in this film are not excessive for the genre, but the film is still most appropriate for an adult audience.

The film contains action violence, scenes of peril, murder, a brief nongraphic sexual scene, partial nudity elsewhere, some innuendo, and rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
